item.title: Cervical Rotation MET
clinicalUse: Pain-limited or muscle-guarded cervical rotation after red-flag screening
stabilization: Support head and control trunk so movement is cervical, not whole-body.
contact: Hands cradle occiput/side of head without compressing jaw or neck vessels.
forceDirection: Move to comfortable rotation barrier; patient gently attempts rotation opposite therapist resistance for isometric contraction.
safety: Avoid in instability, acute trauma, vascular/neurological concern.
item.visualCue: Move to barrier → Gentle isometric hold → Relax → Take up new range.

subTechniques.name: Upper Trapezius — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce painful guarding or improve a side-bending restriction when the upper trapezius is clinically relevant.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine or supported sitting. Gently side-bend the head away from the treated side until the first comfortable resistance is reached; keep the shoulder girdle relaxed.
subTechniques.contact: One hand supports the occiput/head. The other hand controls the superior shoulder so the scapula does not simply elevate.
subTechniques.direction: Ask the patient to gently elevate the shoulder or side-bend the head toward the treated side against matched resistance. After 5–10 seconds, relax fully and take up only the new pain-free range.
subTechniques.dosage: 3–5 low-effort contractions, usually about 10–20% effort. Reposition after each relaxation rather than forcing a stretch.
subTechniques.reassess: Cervical side-bending, rotation, familiar neck pain and shoulder-elevation comfort.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: If the shoulder is not stabilized, the patient can compensate with scapular elevation instead of producing a useful cervical-muscle contraction.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Stop if dizziness, unusual headache, distal neurological symptoms or marked symptom escalation appears.

subTechniques.name: Levator Scapulae — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Improve painful cervical rotation/flexion restriction associated with levator scapulae guarding.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supported sitting or supine. Move the neck gently into flexion, rotation away and slight side-bending away from the treated side until the first comfortable barrier.
subTechniques.contact: Support the head while the other hand controls the superior-medial scapular border/shoulder girdle.
subTechniques.direction: Ask the patient to gently elevate the shoulder blade toward the ear against resistance. Relax, then take up the new comfortable neck/scapular position.
subTechniques.dosage: 3–5 contractions of 5–10 seconds at low effort.
subTechniques.reassess: Cervical rotation, flexion and the patient's familiar upper-medial scapular pain.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Think 'scapula plus neck'—if only the neck is moved, the levator may not be specifically loaded.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid aggressive positioning in acute cervical injury or when neurological/vascular screening is not reassuring.

subTechniques.name: Scalene Group — MET
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce selected scalene guarding and improve comfortable cervical side-bending/respiratory movement.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Supine with the head supported. Place the neck in a small amount of extension or neutral and side-bend away only to the first comfortable barrier.
subTechniques.contact: Support the occiput and stabilize the upper thorax/clavicular region without compressing the anterior neck.
subTechniques.direction: Ask for a very gentle side-bending effort toward the treated side or a controlled inspiratory effort, then relax and take up the new comfortable range.
subTechniques.dosage: 2–4 gentle cycles; use less force than for larger limb muscles.
subTechniques.reassess: Cervical side-bending, first-rib/upper-chest comfort and symptom response with breathing.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: The anterior neck is not a place for heavy manual force. Precision and low effort matter more than strength.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Do not compress the carotid region; stop with dizziness, visual symptoms, dysphagia or neurological change.
